tasks.task: e2e suite stabilisation — route warm-up pass, and review specs that override the config timeout downward (c1 sets `page.setDefaultTimeout(15_000)`)
tasks.notes:
Opened by Day 22, the first CI run. NOT a state bug — `verify-day-c1` failed on CI run 1 and PASSED on run 2 with NO fix applied (only the webhook secret changed), and five escalating local repros against a virgin DB could not reproduce it: alone, after day-19, with .env.local removed, on a cold .next, and in the full 65-spec run. A state bug fails identically; a timing flake does not. KNOWN-FLAKY SET — six specs, all timeouts on navigation/visibility, none an assertion that data was wrong: verify-day-c1, verify-day-c2, verify-day-19 (operator impersonation), verify-day-5, verify-day-6, verify-day-16 (accessibility). verify-day-c2 added from the Day 22 post-merge run on main (run 34126383303): 'a dealer detail page renders its state as a full name' flaked on the row-click navigation — toHaveURL(/dealers/) timed out at 15 s (19× on http://localhost:3000/dealers), passed on retry — same signature. The faithful local repro run scored 61 passed / 3 flaky / 1 failed in 19.1m vs CI 19.4m, so the environments perform comparably and the instability is in the suite, not the runner. TWO PARTS: (1) a route warm-up pass so first-hit dev-server compilation (5–10 s/route, DEV.87) is not competing with test execution; (2) audit specs that TIGHTEN timeouts below the config — c1 sets page.setDefaultTimeout(15_000) against a 60 s config default while walking the heaviest cold-route path in the suite (/admin/tenants/new, /admin/tenants/[id], /change-password, three logins), and its own runtime doubled 14.2 s standalone → 28.7 s at the end of the full run. Sequenced BEFORE the Typst migration: F.38 rewrites the PDF specs and should land on a stable suite. DEV.93. DEV.101 — CI run 34223278188 (PR #3) went red on `e2e` with `"unexpected": 0`: NO test failed. Two known-flake retries (verify-day-19 38.6 s, verify-day-c1 36.9 s) burned 75.5 s, and the suite's own test time was 19.0 min of the 20.0 min `globalTimeout`, so the cap fired mid-run and 2 verify-day-c2 tests never ran. Recent green runs sit at 16m25s–19m10s against that 20 min cap and `main` itself passes at 18.2 min WITH 2 flakies — so two retries can now redden any branch including `main`. Both failures were 15 s navigation timeouts, and `verify-day-c1` sets `page.setDefaultTimeout(15_000)` against a 60 s config default. OPEN FOR THE OPERATOR, not decided: (a) whether "restore headroom against `globalTimeout`" becomes an explicit acceptance criterion here, and (b) whether the 20 min cap is still right — it was sized in DEV.81 to kill a Windows teardown hang, not to bound suite runtime. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (operator-set, Day 23, DEV.102 — measurable, not aspirational): (1) the six known flakes CLASSIFIED timing-vs-state, each with evidence; (2) e2e completes UNDER 15 MINUTES with ZERO retries; (3) no spec skipped, disabled, `fixme`-d, or given a longer timeout to get there. Criterion 2 is the point — without it F.52 ships "fewer flakes" while runtime stays at ~19 min and the gate is straight back where it was. Criterion 3 exists so criterion 2 cannot be met by weakening what is tested. NOTE: `globalTimeout` was raised 20 → 40 min on Day 23 (DEV.102) on its own merits and gives F.52 room to work, but does NOT satisfy criterion 2 — that is measured against actual runtime, not against the cap. DAY 24 PHASE 1 — verify-day-6 CONFIRMED FLAKY ON MAIN, and its signature BREAKS the characterisation above. Post-merge run 34309474851 on main (commit 664cca8 — the run this baseline is read from): 65 tests, 1 worker, 64 passed / 1 flaky / 0 failed, suite 18.5 min, e2e job 19m38s, whole run 22m15s. Against the acceptance criteria that is a FAIL on both halves of criterion 2 — 18.5 min against a sub-15-min target, and one retry against a zero-retry target. The flake was `verify-day-6.spec.ts:45:7 > Day 6 — inventory + procurements > procurement detail page renders for a seeded procurement`, failing at line 54 on `await expect(page.locator("h1")).toContainText(/PROC-/)` — a 15 s CONTENT assertion, NOT a navigation or visibility timeout. verify-day-6 was ALREADY one of the known-flaky six, so this adds evidence rather than a seventh spec; what is new is that the claim above — "all timeouts on navigation/visibility, none an assertion that data was wrong" — no longer holds for the set. Treat that sentence as superseded for verify-day-6. CLASSIFICATION IS GENUINELY OPEN; DO NOT CARRY A GUESS INTO THE TRIAGE. The first read on the day was "state bug — the seeded procurement is not visible to the query". That read is wrong on the evidence, and the operator said why: a state bug of that shape re-runs the SAME query against the SAME database on the retry and fails again. It passed on retry. That is more consistent with the content not being RENDERED yet than with it not EXISTING. But neither reading is to be assumed. A late h1 has a timing explanation (first-hit dev-server route compile, 5-10 s, DEV.87 — the same mechanism part (1) of this task targets) AND a state explanation (a row becoming visible only after an earlier spec commits), and the observable is identical either way. This is precisely what N=5 against a virgin database is for: run flake-triager on verify-day-6, fresh DB, 5 runs, and let the per-run evidence classify it. Criterion 1 requires evidence, not a plausible story. SECOND OBSERVATION — PR #5 (docs-only branch docs/dev-103-merge-gate), run 34327213279, e2e job 102387759938: 63 passed / 2 flaky / 0 failed, suite 17.8 min. Both flakes were known-set specs: verify-day-19.spec.ts:183 (operator impersonation, toHaveURL — the DEV.93/DEV.101 signature) and verify-day-6.spec.ts:45 — the SAME toContainText(/PROC-/) failure at line 54 as the baseline run, again passing on retry. verify-day-6 has now flaked on two consecutive runs, on two different branches, the second from a docs-only diff that touched no spec, no app route and no schema. THE TWO OBSERVATIONS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT, AND THE CLASSIFICATION STAYS OPEN. Both runs execute the same 65 specs in the same order on a single worker, so a state bug seeded by an EARLIER spec's write would clear on the retry in both runs exactly as observed. The repetition raises the reproduction RATE; it does not raise confidence in either classification. What two reproductions do buy is triage economics — verify-day-6 is the cheapest spec in the set to get a verdict on, because it actually reproduces. Runtime for the two runs was 18.5 min and 17.8 min, both with retries burning time, so the gap to criterion 2 is a consistent ~3-4 min structural gap rather than run-to-run noise. TRIAGE ORDER (Day 24 Phase 1, operator-set) — supersedes the listing order of the six above, which was arbitrary: (1) verify-day-6 — two reproductions in two runs on different branches, the strongest signal in the set; (2) verify-day-19 — two reproductions (DEV.101 on PR #3, and PR #5), same toHaveURL signature both times; (3) verify-day-c2 — one reproduction, Day 22 post-merge run 34126383303; (4) verify-day-5; (5) verify-day-16 (accessibility); (6) verify-day-c1 — LAST, and deliberately so. c1 has not reproduced since DEV.93: five escalating local repros against a virgin DB failed to reproduce it, and it passed on CI run 2 with no fix applied. It may cost N runs to tell us nothing, so it is not where the first budget goes. This inverts the old order, in which c1 led because it was the first flake seen, not because it was the most tractable. The ordering of (2)-(5) was not operator-specified: it is by reproduction count, then by whether the failure has a recorded signature. Reorder freely if a run changes the evidence. CLOSED Day 24. BOTH acceptance criteria met, and the day's own theory of the cause was wrong. CRITERION 2 MET ON CI: PR #6, run 34391508643 — `65 passed (9.3m)`, ZERO flaky, ZERO failed, e2e job 11m58s (was 17m40s on run 34375881563). ROOT CAUSE was NOT first-hit route compilation. It was Next dev ON-DEMAND-ENTRIES EVICTION: `pagesBufferLength: 5` and `maxInactiveAge: 60s` against a suite that visits ~40 routes over a 16-19 minute run, so almost every route was evicted and recompiled repeatedly — measured locally `/login` 5x, `/dashboard` 5x, `/dealers/[id]` 4x, and on CI run 34375881563 `/dealers` and `/dealers/[id]` 3x each with module counts VARYING between compiles (5464 -> 4307 -> 4429), which is eviction and rebuild, not a server restart. Each recompile costs 8-16s on CI and lands on whichever test touches the route next, against a 15s expect budget. FIX = two coupled changes: `onDemandEntries` in apps/web/next.config.mjs (dev-only keys; `next build` ignores them, so it cannot reach production — a deliberate scope call recorded in DEV.105) plus the mandated route warm-up pass in apps/web/tests/e2e/global-setup.ts. MEASURED BEFORE KEEPING, workers:1, virgin DB each run: baseline 18.8min (63 passed/1 flaky/1 FAILED); warm-up ONLY 21.3min (62 passed/2 flaky/1 FAILED) — the mandated fix SHIPPED ALONE MADE THE SUITE SLOWER, because eviction discarded it; onDemandEntries only 9.4min then 9.3min on repeat (65 passed, 0 flaky); BOTH 6.9min (65 passed, 0 flaky). The warm-up was kept only because it then earned its place: in the final configuration ALL compilation completes during warm-up and ZERO compiles occur during the test phase, versus 44 still landing inside test budgets without it. Confirmed on CI: 17 compiles total, 0 after `Running 65 tests`, 0 restarts, one server lifetime. CRITERION 3 HELD: no spec skipped, disabled, fixme-d or given a longer timeout. Three specs had a `page.setDefaultTimeout` BELOW the config default with no stated reason (verify-day-c1:54, operator-onboarding:72 at 15s; verify-day-19:186 at 30s) — REMOVED, not raised; operator-onboarding failed on exactly that 15s budget in the baseline run and got further on retry. The two overrides that DO carry a stated reason (operator-readonly-view:31, critical-path:140) were left alone. CRITERION 1 — the six classified: verify-day-6 TIMING FLAKE with the mechanism established positively by flake-triager (the click is an RSC SOFT navigation, so `page.locator('h1')` keeps resolving the LIST page's `

Procurements

` until the transition commits; 19 resolutions across 15s is a compile longer than the expect budget; there is no prefetch in dev so the click is the route's first hit); verify-day-19 TIMING FLAKE, three reproductions all on :183 `toHaveURL`, including one local pre-fix (attempt 0 failed 89.5s, attempt 1 PASSED 7.3s — retry got further, the DEV.93 signature); verify-day-c1 / operator-onboarding TIMING FLAKE, reproduced locally pre-fix with the retry getting further (attempt 0 `page.goto` 15000ms, attempt 1 `page.waitForURL` 15000ms one step later); verify-day-c2 TIMING FLAKE on CI run 34126383303, `toHaveURL` on /dealers/[id] at 15s, passed on retry. verify-day-5 and verify-day-16: NOT REPRODUCED, N=5 each, and BOTH triagers independently reported that their place on the list rests on nothing substantiable — no CI reproduction, and no failure in any of six full-suite runs on Day 24. DELISTING THEM IS AN OPEN OPERATOR DECISION, deliberately not taken here. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, do not let it be lost: the local `verify-day-6` failures on Day 24 were `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED` from a dev-server memory restart (DEV.106), which is a DIFFERENT failure mode from CI's `toContainText(/PROC-/)` — the local instrument was reproducing a local environment fault, not the CI flake, and every post-fix NOT REPRODUCED verdict was taken under warmed, non-evicting, raised-heap conditions and says nothing about pre-fix behaviour. CONFIDENCE, STATED HONESTLY: runtime and compile counts are solid (five full-suite runs, two of the same configuration agreeing within 4 seconds, plus CI). Flake ELIMINATION is not proven — three consecutive clean runs is three runs. The claim is that the mechanism is understood and removed, not that the suite has been observed stable long enough. DEV.104 (globalTimeout inversion), DEV.105 (eviction + scope call), DEV.106 (local-only memory restart), DEV.107 (agents proven, resolves DEV.96), DEV.108 (parallelism NOT raised). RECLASSIFIED Day 24 follow-up: verify-day-5 and verify-day-16 are NOT delisted from the known-flaky six — delisting would imply they were fixed, and they were never demonstrated broken. They are moved to an explicit WATCH — NEVER EVIDENCED state, tracked as F.62. See F.62 for the reasoning and for what a future appearance of either should be treated as. Also corrected: this task's completedDate was 2026-09-09 (session start) and is now 2026-09-10, the date of commit e373a8d which actually marked it complete. RUNTIME WATCH, opened by the operator after the PR #7 merge: e2e came in at 10m7s on the final PR #7 run (CI run 34498478642, suite `65 passed (9.1m)`), against 9.4-9.5m on the three runs before it. One observation, still comfortably inside the 15-minute acceptance criterion and inside the 25-minute globalTimeout, and not a regression on any evidence available — but it is the FIRST run above ten minutes since the fix landed, so 9.5m should not be assumed to be the steady state. WHAT TO WATCH, and why it is not obviously noise: the job wall-clock and the suite's own reported time can move independently, because the job also carries ~1 min of install/browser-install/migrate/seed plus the ~100-120s route warm-up in global-setup.ts, and the warm-up's own cost varies with GitHub runner CPU (measured 106.0s, 119.1s, 119.1s across three runs). So a rising job time with a flat suite time means the warm-up or the setup got slower, while a rising SUITE time would mean compilation has started leaking back into the test phase — which is the thing F.52 actually fixed and the only one of the two that would matter. The diagnostic that separates them is already in the logs and costs nothing: count `Compiled /` lines occurring AFTER `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job. The fix's signature is ZERO (confirmed on runs 34391508643 and 34426329250: 17 compiles total, all during warm-up, none during the test phase). A non-zero count on a future run means on-demand-entries eviction has returned — check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that nothing has raised the route count past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Do NOT respond to a slow run by raising a timeout; that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. RUNTIME WATCH CLOSED by the operator after six post-fix CI runs. THE STEADY STATE IS A BAND, NOT A POINT: 9.1-9.7 min of suite time (runs 34391508643, 34426329250, 34492261635, 34498478642, 34569838273, 34581641886), with job wall-clock 10m7s-11m58s. Treat 9.1-9.7 as the band and do NOT treat 9.5 as a point estimate — the earlier 10m7s observation that opened this watch was inside normal variance, not a regression, and the variance lives in the job rather than the suite (the warm-up's own cost has measured 106.0s / 119.1s / 119.1s / 121.7s with runner CPU). THE SIGNATURE HELD ON EVERY RUN CHECKED: zero `Compiled /` lines after `Running 65 tests`, zero dev-server restarts, one server lifetime. STOP TRACKING THIS. Resume only on one of exactly two signals, which are the two that would mean on-demand-entries eviction has returned: (1) a run exceeding 11 MINUTES of suite time, or (2) ANY `Compiled /` line appearing after `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job log. Either one means check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that the route count has not grown past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Neither signal is a timeout problem and neither is to be answered by raising a timeout — that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. Routine run-to-run jitter inside the band is not a signal and should not be investigated.

tasks.task: packages/tax `GstRate` union omits 3% — type-versus-runtime mismatch on a protected surface
tasks.notes: `packages/tax/src/types.ts:7` declares `export type GstRate = 0 | 5 | 12 | 18 | 28;` — no 3. The database disagrees: `products_gst_rate_chk`, `quotation_lines_gst_rate_chk`, `performa_invoice_lines_gst_rate_chk` and `order_lines_gst_rate_chk` all read `IN (0, 3, 5, 12, 18, 28)` (packages/db/src/schema/product.ts:72, quotation.ts:171, performa-invoice.ts:175, order.ts:172), and CLAUDE.md §5 states the allowed rates as `0, 3, 5, 12, 18, 28`. So a 3% row is legal in Postgres, legal per the spec, and unrepresentable in the tax engine's own type. The doc comment above the union also cites the wrong section — it says 'per CLAUDE.md §6' where the rates live in §5. WHY THIS MATTERS AND WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX: F.3 (multi-rate tax summary, days 35) groups and keys by rate, and CLAUDE.md §5 already warns that `gst_rate` arrives from the driver as a STRING ('18' vs '18.00'), so grouping must normalise to a number first. A union that silently excludes 3 is the second half of that trap — a 3% group would be dropped or mistyped rather than double-counted, which is harder to notice. `packages/tax` is a PROTECTED SURFACE under CLAUDE.md §10.1 and docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md §9: widening the union changes the exhaustiveness of every `switch` and every `Record<GstRate, …>` that consumes it, so this needs its own scoped change with the tax suite re-run, not a drive-by edit. Raised Day 24 during F.52; deliberately NOT fixed that day. Sequence it BEFORE F.3.

tasks.task: e2e test isolation — three specs mutate shared seeded rows selected by `.first()`, which blocks any CI parallelism increase
tasks.notes: Opened by Day 24 (F.52) after Phase 3.3's interdependence check came back POSITIVE, so `workers` was left at 1 and 2/3 were never measured — per the day's own instruction to report interdependence rather than raise workers through it. `fullyParallel` is false, so raising workers parallelises across FILES while every worker shares one database. PARALLEL-SAFE, already checked and cleared: the two tenant-provisioning specs cannot collide (verify-day-c1.spec.ts:24 and operator-onboarding.spec.ts:41 derive slug/GSTIN/PAN/email from Date.now() at module load, with DIFFERENT PAN prefixes AABCR vs AABCA at :46 and :64); verify-day-19's rate-limit probe is keyed per worker PROCESS (`f19-e2e-${process.pid}-${Date.now()}@demo.test`, :43); operator impersonation is COOKIE-scoped (`dealerlink_impersonation`, apps/web/lib/tenant/context.ts:16); document numbering is atomic by design. THE THREE THAT ARE NOT SAFE: (1) verify-day-13.spec.ts:60-68 takes the FIRST dispatchable order matching `ORD-\d{4}-` — a pattern chosen to dodge DB-test residue, but critical-path.spec.ts:320 creates a real order through the live counter that matches it too; (2) verify-day-13.spec.ts:87+ flips the FIRST in-transit dispatch to delivered, and critical-path's own dispatch is in-transit and a candidate; (3) verify-day-12.spec.ts:58+ takes the FIRST pending_verification payment, and critical-path.spec.ts:343-347 creates a payment in exactly that state — the most likely collision of the three. This is the DEV.31 residue pattern between two CONCURRENT specs rather than two sequential suites, and the resulting failure would be non-deterministic and would look exactly like a flake, which is the specific outcome F.52 existed to remove. A FOURTH hazard was found by flake-triager during the Day 24 triage and is latent rather than active: verify-day-19's `cleanupProbe()` deletes auth_events rows by `metadata LIKE '%PROBE_EMAIL%'`, but its own `login_failed` rows carry the literal metadata `no_user_or_inactive` with no email in it, so they accumulate (12 -> 30 rows over five runs). Benign under serial execution because the assertions read the newest row and every accumulated row says the same thing — but the queries at :141-148 and :171-176 are ordered `desc` and scoped by EVENT TYPE only, not by the probe key, so under concurrency they would read another worker's row and fail as a CONTENT mismatch, i.e. it would present as a state bug. WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS: make those specs create the rows they mutate instead of selecting a seeded `.first()`, scope verify-day-19's auth_events queries by probe key, then re-measure at workers 2 and 3. NOTE THE PRIORITY HAS DROPPED SHARPLY: Phase 3's premise was that workers:1 costs runtime worth reclaiming, and after F.52 it does not — the suite runs in 9.3 min on CI against a 15-minute target. This is now a correctness/robustness task, not a speed one, and should be sequenced accordingly.

tasks.task: WATCH — verify-day-5 and verify-day-16 were never evidenced as flaky; treat any future failure as NEW signal
tasks.notes: Opened by the Day 24 follow-up. These two specs were carried on the known-flaky six for the whole of Stage F and NOTHING EVER SUBSTANTIATED THAT. There is no CI reproduction of either. Neither failed in ANY of the six full-suite runs on Day 24. flake-triager ran each at N=5 and returned NOT REPRODUCED both times, and in both reports reached the same unprompted conclusion — that their place on the list 'rests on nothing I could confirm' (verify-day-5) and 'rests on nothing I can substantiate' (verify-day-16). WHY THIS IS A WATCH AND NOT A DELISTING, which is the whole point of the task: delisting would record them as FIXED. They were never shown to be broken, so there is nothing to have fixed, and a 'fixed' record would be a false statement in the plan. Equally they were not shown to be healthy — the N=5 runs were taken under POST-FIX conditions (warmed routes, onDemandEntries preventing eviction, 6144 MB heap ceiling), which is the condition LEAST likely to reproduce a compile-timing failure, and both triagers said so explicitly and declined to call the specs healthy. THE OPERATIONAL RULE THIS TASK EXISTS TO CARRY: if verify-day-5 or verify-day-16 fails on any future run, it is NEW SIGNAL and must be triaged as a first-time failure. It must NOT be waved through as 'one of the known flakes', because there is no evidence behind that label and treating it as a known-flake shrug would discard the first real data either spec has ever produced. Close this task only when either (a) one of them produces a genuine reproduction, at which point it becomes a real classification with real evidence, or (b) enough post-fix runs accumulate that 'never evidenced' can be retired on a stated number of green runs rather than on the absence of anyone looking. A LATENT ISSUE worth knowing if either does fail: verify-day-5 (lines 11-13, 22-24) and verify-day-16 (line 16, and line 70's 'No seeded orders' guard) both carry test.skip guards that would make them SKIP GREEN rather than fail if the seeded admin ever needed password rotation or the seeded rows went missing — so a pass/fail count alone can hide a state change in either spec. flake-triager confirmed the guards did NOT fire during its runs (verify-day-16: 'skipped: 0' on all five runs, the same seeded order id fetched all five times), but the exposure is structural and remains.

tasks.task: Make PROJECT_PLAN.md ENTIRELY generated — move the narrative out, so no hand-editable region remains (folded into F.37)
tasks.notes: Opened by the Day 24 follow-up, on `verifier`'s recommendation (DEV.113). THE PROBLEM: `PROJECT_PLAN.md` carries Stage 0 and Stages A-E, plus all headings, OUTSIDE the `STAGE_F_TASKS` markers. `.claude/agents/verifier.md` now says no change outside the markers is permitted, full stop. But `.claude/settings.json` denies `Edit`/`Write` on the file, CLAUDE.md §10.4 says it is 'never hand-edited, by any agent, ever', and `pnpm plan:sync` only writes between the markers. So the file is simultaneously REQUIRED to change eventually and UNCHANGEABLE by any approved route. A Stage G heading, a stage retitle, a typo fix in a Stage A row, or the A-E restructure implied by F.37 and F.56-F.60 are all legitimate and all currently forbidden. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: left alone, the DEV.112 situation recurs verbatim — correct verifier FAIL, operator overrule, another unsatisfiability entry — until overrule becomes routine and CLAUDE.md §10.3 erodes. That erosion is exactly what DEV.112 worked hardest to prevent, so this task is the defence of that entry, not a retreat from it. VERIFIER'S RECOMMENDATION, on record in its Day 24 report and NOT yet adopted: separate the invariant that actually matters — generated content is never hand-edited, and `plan:sync` never clobbers authored content — from its current over-approximation, which is 'nothing outside the markers may change'. Make an out-of-marker edit SATISFIABLE BUT EXPENSIVE AND VISIBLE rather than forbidden: its own commit, touching only `PROJECT_PLAN.md`, a conventional token in the commit message, and a DEVIATIONS entry referencing it; the verifier then checks every out-of-marker changed line belongs to a so-tagged commit and that the entry exists. Tighten the complement so it is not a loophole — inside such a commit the generated region must be byte-identical, and the `## Changelog` ban stays absolute and independently enforced by scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts. The §10.4 / settings.json inconsistency must be fixed in the SAME change or the rule amendment is dead on arrival: scope §10.4 to 'the generated block is never hand-edited' and give the operator a recorded path while keeping the agent-level Edit/Write denial. EXPLICITLY REJECTED by the verifier, do not reach for it: 'allow out-of-marker changes when the operator approves' — that is the precedent DEV.112 refused to set and it reduces the rule to a formality. LONGER-RUN ALTERNATIVE, noted and not recommended next: bring the whole document under `plan:sync` so no out-of-marker region exists and the rule is trivially satisfiable forever — cleaner end state, more work, and it makes the historical A-E tables JSON-editable, which carries its own review cost. THIS IS A DECISION-BEARING CHANGE to a gate's pass condition and to CLAUDE.md: main-thread work per §10.4, and the operator's call per §10.1. Not urgent today; certain to bite. DECIDED BY THE OPERATOR, Day 24 follow-up: ELIMINATE THE HYBRID. Do NOT sanction a permitted-edit path. The reasoning, recorded because it is the part worth keeping: a permitted-edit path reintroduces exactly the drift the deny exists to prevent, and routine overrule turns CLAUDE.md §10.3 into a formality. DEV.112 also OVERCLAIMED — its 'exactly one commit in this repository's history must fail this check' is false going forward, because ANY legitimate out-of-marker change fails the rule, and the queued docs work already contains one: POST_PILOT_WORK_ORDER.md §1.5 wants PROJECT_PLAN.md updated to record that Stage E never completed and that UMA is on hold. That is a real, legitimate, currently-impossible edit, not a hypothetical. THE SHAPE OF THE FIX: (1) move the narrative — Stage 0, Stages A-E, and Risks & Open Items — into a normally-editable file (docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md or similar), where ordinary editing rules apply and no deny rule is needed at all; (2) `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` renders the WHOLE of PROJECT_PLAN.md from `docs/stage-f-tasks.json` plus a small committed header template; (3) the verifier rule becomes 'no hand edits at all' rather than 'none outside the markers' — trivially satisfiable forever, with no out-of-marker region left to argue about; (4) the `Edit`/`Write` deny in `.claude/settings.json` becomes unqualified and CORRECT rather than a blunt instrument with a known dead zone; (5) the Changelog guard's form-specificity stops mattering — `not.toMatch(/^##\s+Changelog\s*$/m)` would not catch `### Changelog` or `## Changelog — restored`, and a fully generated file cannot acquire a section by hand, so the gap closes structurally rather than by widening the regex. FOLDED INTO F.37, same PR: F.37 is already moving build history into docs/archive/ with `git mv`, so this is the same shape of work on the same files at the same time. Doing it separately would mean two restructures of the same documents. HONEST COST, stated rather than buried: roughly a day, and `sync-project-plan.ts` ends up owning more than the Stage F task table — it becomes the renderer for the whole document, which is more surface in one script. That is smaller than living with a file that structurally cannot be maintained. SUPERSEDES the 'VERIFIER'S RECOMMENDATION, not yet adopted' paragraph above: that recommendation was to make an out-of-marker edit satisfiable-but-expensive, and the operator rejected it for the reason given at the top of this decision. The verifier's own 'longer-run alternative' — bring the whole document under plan:sync — is what was chosen. Its one stated objection to that, that it makes the historical A-E tables JSON-editable, is answered by moving the narrative to a plain markdown file instead of into JSON. THIRD INSTANCE, and the operator's judgement is that it is the SHARPEST of the three: `PROJECT_PLAN.md:3` still reads 'Append a dated entry to the changelog at the bottom every time you mark something done.' The `## Changelog` section it refers to was deleted on Day 24 (DEV.110), so line 3 is now a STANDING WRITTEN INSTRUCTION TO PERFORM THE FORBIDDEN EDIT — the edit CLAUDE.md §10.4 forbids, `.claude/settings.json` denies, and the verifier's containment check fails. WHAT MAKES IT THE SHARPEST: line 3 sits OUTSIDE the `STAGE_F_TASKS` markers, so correcting the instruction is ITSELF blocked by the rule the instruction violates. The document cannot be brought into a consistent state from inside its own rules. That is not a rule with a gap — it is the argument for the fix. A sed to correct line 3 was offered to the operator on Day 24 and deliberately not applied by the main thread, because applying it would have required exactly the out-of-marker hand edit under discussion. HOW FULL GENERATION RESOLVES IT, BY CONSTRUCTION RATHER THAN BY CORRECTION: once `PROJECT_PLAN.md` is rendered in its entirety, line 3 becomes part of the committed header template, so it is PRODUCED correctly on every sync rather than needing to be fixed in place. There is no edit to authorise, no exception to carve, and no stale instruction to remember to chase — the inconsistency cannot exist in a generated file because the generator is the only thing that writes the line. Note this also means the header template must be written with line 3 already corrected: do not port the current text across verbatim, or the fix ships the defect it was meant to remove. The three known instances to check against the finished template are (1) POST_PILOT_WORK_ORDER.md §1.5's request to record that Stage E never completed and UMA is on hold, (2) the Stage 0 / Stage A-E / Risks narrative itself, and (3) this line 3 instruction.

tasks.task: Harden `plan-keeper` against any git state mutation, and fix the main-thread race that triggered one
tasks.notes: Opened by DEV.114. WHAT HAPPENED: the main thread invoked `plan-keeper`, then committed the resulting working-tree changes BEFORE the agent had reported. The agent, still running, found a commit it had not made, correctly judged it inconsistent with its own prohibition on committing, and ran `git reset HEAD~1` to undo it. The commit vanished; the edits survived unstaged; the work was re-committed afterwards. No data was lost. TWO SEPARATE FIXES, and the second matters more than the first. (1) THE RACE, main-thread side: never commit a subagent's output until that subagent has reported. This is a workflow rule and belongs in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md alongside the C7a ordering rule added the same day — the same class of defect, an ordering assumption held in someone's head rather than written down. (2) THE REMIT GAP, agent side: `plan-keeper`'s hard limits enumerate `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, and creating a branch or PR. `git reset` is not on that list, and the enumeration is exactly what let this through. Replace the list with a blanket prohibition on ANY git state mutation — reset, checkout, revert, stash, cherry-pick, branch -f, rebase — and add the standing instruction: if you find a commit you did not make, REPORT IT and stop; never repair it. An agent whose remit is 'edit one JSON file' must not be able to move HEAD on any reasoning, including correct reasoning, and its reasoning here WAS correct, which is what makes the gap worth closing rather than excusing. RELATED OBSERVATION from the same invocation, bearing on how much to trust an unreviewed agent: the safety classifier was reported unavailable for it, so its output went unreviewed. The main thread verified the JSON independently before re-committing (63 tasks, F.52 still complete with completedDate 2026-09-10, no duplicate ids, no invalid statuses, diff confined to the two lines of the notes field) and the edit was clean. Verifying because a guard reported itself absent is the right order of operations and should be the documented habit. OPERATOR DIRECTION, Day 24 follow-up — SUPERSEDES the 'replace the list with a blanket prohibition' wording above on the mechanism, though not on the intent: implement an ALLOW-LIST of permitted git operations, not a deny-list of remembered prohibited ones. A prohibition list will always have gaps — `git reset` was missing from exactly such a list and that gap is the whole incident. State positively what `plan-keeper` may run (read-only inspection: `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, `git ls-files`) and treat everything else as forbidden by default, including commands nobody thought to name. The same reasoning applies to the other agents' prompts, which all carry enumerated prohibitions — worth sweeping while in there, though only `plan-keeper` has a write tool and therefore the real blast radius.

tasks.task: `grep` returns silent false negatives in the devcontainer — audit the negative-existence claims that depend on it
tasks.notes: Opened by DEV.115, found by `verifier` while re-deriving its own evidence. THE FAULT: on `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts`, `grep` returned exit 1 with NO OUTPUT for strings demonstrably present in the file — including `MARKER_START` and `Changelog` — while `sed` and `node` read the same content correctly. It worked normally on other paths (PROJECT_PLAN.md, DEVIATIONS.md, scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts). So it fails SILENTLY AND SELECTIVELY, on some paths and not others, with no error and no diagnostic. WHY THIS IS THE WORST FAILURE MODE FOR THIS PROJECT: a large share of Stage F's conclusions are negative existence claims derived from a clean grep — 'no globalSetup anywhere', 'zero restart markers across four CI runs', 'Grep absent from the toolset', 'no ## Changelog in main'. A tool that silently reports 'not found' for content that is present can manufacture any of those, and nothing in the output distinguishes a true negative from a broken read. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN TO SURVIVE, corroborated by non-grep means: absence of recompiles during the test phase (confirmed by `Compiled /` counts read two ways in CI logs AND by the measured runtime drop 18.8min -> 9.3min); the agent tool-grant mismatches (confirmed by agents enumerating their own function schemas, not by grep); the changelog's absence from main (confirmed by `node` line counts). NOT DIAGNOSED and deliberately not guessed: no cause is claimed. A binary or locale issue, a file-encoding interaction and a sandbox filesystem quirk were all considered and NONE was investigated. Do not write a cause into this task without reproducing it. OPERATIONAL RULE to adopt meanwhile, and the cheapest part of this task: do not accept a negative grep result on its own as proof of absence — confirm with `node`, `sed`, or `git grep`. That belongs in docs/RUNBOOKS.md and in the read-only agents' prompts, several of which instruct the agent to 'grep it and quote it'. SMALL RESIDUE found by the same agent via `node` after grep failed on the file: `INSERT_BEFORE_HEADINGS` in scripts/sync-project-plan.ts still lists `'## Changelog'` as an insertion anchor. Dead today — the markers exist, so the creation path never runs — but it is a live reference to a now-banned section that would quietly re-anchor insertion if the section ever returned. Remove it as part of this task. PRIORITY, set by the operator Day 24 follow-up: keep this ABOVE COSMETIC. It is not a tooling annoyance. `code-auditor` and `doc-auditor` both reason from grep as their primary instrument, and a silent false negative there produces a CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER rather than a visible failure — an agent reports 'DOES NOT EXIST' with file:line evidence for everything it did find, and nothing in its output distinguishes that from a broken read. Every EXISTS/DOES NOT EXIST verdict in the Stage F record inherits this risk. Visible failures are cheap; confidently wrong verdicts get built on. NARROWED since the entry was written: the verifier reproduced the fault and characterised its blast radius — on `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts`, `grep -c MARKER_START` returns exit 1 with no output while `git grep` reports 4 and `node` and `sed` independently count 4; on `PROJECT_PLAN.md`, `DEVIATIONS.md`, `docs/stage-f-tasks.json` and `scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts` grep and node agree line-for-line. So it is at least file-specific rather than universal, which makes it more dangerous, not less: a tool that is usually right is trusted. `git grep` worked where `grep` did not, which is a candidate mitigation worth testing before any deeper diagnosis. ROOT CAUSE FOUND, Day 24 follow-up — and it is NOT a sandbox fault, NOT selective-by-path mystery, and NOT a grep bug. `scripts/sync-project-plan.ts` CONTAINS A LITERAL NUL BYTE, at offset 9441, line 264, inside the template literal in `outsideMarkers()`: `return \`${plan.slice(0, pos.start)}\0${plan.slice(pos.end + MARKER_END.length)}\``. It is DELIBERATE and documented — the function's own docstring calls it 'a sentinel standing in for the generated content', and comparing outside-markers before and after is how the verifier proves the script touched nothing else. GNU grep treats ANY file containing a NUL byte as BINARY and suppresses matches, which is the entire observed behaviour: exit 1, no output, no warning. PROOF, four instruments on the same file and pattern: `node` counts 4 occurrences of `MARKER_START`; plain `grep -c` exits 1 with no output; `grep -ac` (force text) returns 4; `git grep -c` returns 4; `rg -c` returns 4. `LC_ALL=C` makes no difference, ruling out the locale/multibyte theory. THE BLAST RADIUS IS ONE FILE, and this is the reassuring part: a sweep of every git-tracked file for NUL bytes returns exactly this script plus genuine binaries (2 PDFs, a .docx, 5 PNGs, 2 sample PDFs). Every other text file in the repo greps correctly, which matches the verifier's earlier observation that grep agreed with node on PROJECT_PLAN.md, DEVIATIONS.md and the test file. So NO Stage F conclusion is at risk unless it grepped THIS script — and the audits were about app routes, schemas, CI logs and specs, none of which touch it. THE CONCLUSION THAT MATTERED MOST WAS RE-VERIFIED ANYWAY: see F.6. MITIGATION ALREADY SHIPPED (Day 24 follow-up): the four Bash-holding agents — doc-auditor, ci-investigator, flake-triager — now carry an explicit search-instrument section directing `git grep` first, `rg` second, `node -e` third, and plain `grep` as CORROBORATION ONLY, never the sole basis for a negative, with `-a` if used at all; doc-auditor's Permitted Bash list was updated to match. code-auditor got the opposite note: its dedicated `Grep` tool is RIPGREP-BACKED and was NEVER AFFECTED, it has no Bash so it cannot reach the broken path, and it was verified correct on this very file — so the instruction there is to keep using it and to stop resting any DOES NOT EXIST on a single search. THE REMAINING FIX, one line, NOT YET DONE and needing an operator decision because it touches the script the plan gate depends on: change the sentinel in `outsideMarkers()` from `\0` to any non-NUL improbable value (a printable token, or `\u0001`). Any sentinel works — it is only ever compared against itself, before versus after — and it eliminates the fault at source rather than routing around it. SEQUENCING NOTE: F.37/F.63 is about to rewrite this script wholesale to render the whole document, so the cheapest moment is inside that change, not before it. Also fold in the previously-noted residue: `INSERT_BEFORE_HEADINGS` still lists `'## Changelog'` as an insertion anchor (line 58), dead today but a live reference to a banned section. CORRECTION, same day, caught by `verifier` before the PR opened. THE 'ROOT CAUSE FOUND' PARAGRAPH ABOVE MISATTRIBUTES THE FAILING TOOL. The NUL byte is real and everything said about it holds — offset 9441, line 264, the deliberate sentinel in `outsideMarkers()`, and the blast radius of exactly one tracked source file plus genuine binaries (independently re-confirmed by a sweep of all 666 tracked files: 11 contain a NUL — 4 PDFs, 1 .docx, 5 PNGs, and this script). WHAT IS WRONG IS THE NAME OF THE BROKEN INSTRUMENT. It is NOT GNU grep. In a Claude Code session `grep` is a SHELL FUNCTION SHIM installed by the harness, backed by UGREP (7.8.4 observed, aarch64). That shim is what exits 1 with no output on a NUL-bearing file. Real GNU grep 3.8 at `/usr/bin/grep` handles the same file and pattern CORRECTLY — returns 4, exit 0 — and with `-n` it prints `binary file matches` and still exits 0, i.e. it is honest about what it is doing. Measured, pattern `MARKER_START`, true count 4 per node: bare `grep -c` exit 1 empty; `grep -ac` 4; `/usr/bin/grep -c` 4 exit 0; `git grep -c` 4 with lines; `rg -c` 4 but `rg -n` prints `binary file matches` and lists NO lines without `-a`; `LC_ALL=C` changes nothing. THE SELF-REFUTATION WAS ALREADY IN THE RECORD AND WAS MISSED: the original paragraph noted 'no Binary file matches line' as part of the symptom. That absence was precisely the evidence it was not GNU grep, because GNU grep does print that line. WHY THE MISATTRIBUTION MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A PEDANTIC FIX: (1) the failure is SESSION-SCOPED to the Claude Code shim, so it DOES NOT EXIST IN CI, which has no shim — describing it as a repo-and-binary property overstates where it applies; (2) a future agent that tests `/usr/bin/grep`, sees the correct count and exit 0, would reasonably conclude the whole warning is stale and discount it; (3) it misdirects remediation toward the NUL byte — which is deliberate, documented and correct — instead of toward instrument choice, which is the thing actually under anyone's control. SECOND DEFECT FIXED IN THE SAME PASS: the agent prompts' step 2 recommended `rg -n`, which does not list lines on a NUL-bearing file. Corrected to `rg -na`. All four agent prompts were rewritten with the correct attribution, the measured comparison table, and explicit warnings that the property is session-scoped and that `/usr/bin/grep` working does not make the guidance stale. The one-line sentinel fix remains the real elimination and remains sequenced into F.37/F.63. Recorded in DEV.118, which corrects DEV.117.
